label: rule_on
prompt_text:
Turn the analytical findings below into clear, concise prose for a senior government official.

Do not rewrite each finding separately. Identify overlapping or repeated findings, consolidate them into a small number of underlying patterns, and explain those patterns as a coherent narrative. It is very important that you do not make causal claims - none of our data can be used to determine causality. Do not fabricate or overstate data.

Preserve important numbers and exceptions where useful. Ignore ranking metadata such as "not in the ranked shortlist." Avoid database-style language and do not infer causes that are not supported by the findings.

After every figure and every claim, tag the finding it comes from with its id in square brackets, exactly as given, e.g. [1-00235]. A sentence drawing on two findings carries both tags.

Use figures exactly as they appear in the findings. Do not compute new numbers — no percentages, sums, or differences that are not stated in a finding.

Return only the finished prose.

results.tagged:
Kandhamal’s figures cover only Khajuripada block and one Gram Panchayat in the sample, not the district as a whole [p-district-318-I4][p-district-318-J-3790]. The sample records 573 planned activities [p-district-318-A1] with a planned cost of Rs 3.48 crore [p-district-318-A3]. Sanctions on file total Rs 1.14 crore, the lowest of the 9 districts sampled [p-district-318-A4]. Recorded spending on planned activities is Rs 58.17 lakh [p-district-318-A5], or 16.7% of planned cost, also the lowest share among the 9 districts [p-district-318-A6]. In 2025-2026, recorded spending was Rs 5.10 lakh against Rs 1.06 crore planned, or 4.8% [p-district-318-B-2025-2026].

The first review priority is to reconcile plans, approvals and payments. No cost is recorded for 241 activities (42.1%) [p-district-318-A2]; 167 of those were planned in 2023-2024 [d3-01271]. A scheme is missing for 437 activities (76.3%) [d1-15304], and a fund component is missing for 437 activities (76.3%) [d1-15325]. Administrative approvals are on file for 136 activities (23.7%); a missing record does not establish that approval was never given [p-district-318-F1]. For the works review, start with the 42 works planned in 2022-2023 or earlier that are still marked ongoing: Rs 24.82 lakh of their Rs 38.51 lakh planned cost has been spent (64.4%) [p-district-318-E5]. Check current status against site evidence: only 75 activities have photos on file, the fewest among the 9 districts sampled [p-district-318-E4]. Of the 132 works marked ongoing [p-district-318-E1], the largest groups are Water Sufficient Village (53) and Clean and Green Village (37) [d1-15124].

For the budget review, drinking water is the largest planned spending area at Rs 89.50 lakh, followed by maintenance of community systems at Rs 68.83 lakh [d1-15134]. The tied grant plan is split between drinking water (57.6%) and sanitation (42.4%) [d1-15135], while Self-sufficient Infrastructure in Village accounts for 67.9% (Rs 1.90 crore) of planned untied grants [d1-15114].

results.question: Which blocks stand out on expenditure?
results.tagged:
In the sampled Gram Panchayats, **Bhubaneswar and Rangeilunda are the first blocks to review for overall expenditure**: they appear among the leaders on 5/9 measures [2-00216]. Neither dominates reported spending: Bhubaneswar accounts for 13.1% (Rs 3.33 crore) [d3-00024], and Rangeilunda for 10.8% (Rs 2.73 crore) [d3-00024]. They are also the top two for spending linked to planned activities, at Rs 3.26 crore and Rs 2.57 crore, respectively [d2-00011]. Bhubaneswar recorded the highest cashbook payments in 4/6 fiscal years [2-00260], with 2024-2025 and 2025-2026 as exceptions [2-00260]. Rangeilunda had the largest gap against plan (Rs 9.11 crore below plan) [d4-00109], followed by Kalimela (Rs 5.90 crore below plan) [d4-00109].

**Barpali and Bheden stand out on a different set of measures.** Bheden was among the leaders on 6/9 measures [2-00155], while Barpali was among the leaders on the exceptions: spending linked to planned activities, sanction records and sanctioned amounts [2-00155]. Rangeilunda led on spending linked to planned activities in 2020-2021 (Rs 16.28 lakh) [d2-01034]; Barpali led in 2021-2022 (Rs 76.26 lakh) [d2-01111]. Neither block, nor Bheden, followed the quarter-by-quarter increase in linked spending seen in 9/16 blocks [2-00243]. The recorded share of spending linked to plans rose from 2.7% to 53.2% over six years [d2-00011]; check linked amounts against cashbook totals before treating increases as higher expenditure [d2-00011].

**Khallikote and Laxmipur merit a more targeted review of how expenditure is distributed.** Khallikote was the only block where the comparison of spending with plan was uneven across fund components [1-00307], and it joined Laxmipur as an exception to the generally even spread across work types when spending was compared with sanctions [1-00349]. These exceptions concern the distribution of spending, not its size [1-00307][1-00349]. Ongoing works accounted for most voucher-linked spending in 14/16 blocks [1-00260]; Laxmipur and Boipariguda showed no clear pattern by work status [1-00260].

results.question: What is unusual about water supply works?
results.tagged:
Drinking water and sanitation lead in planned tied grants in 19/20 sampled Gram Panchayats [1-01807], but they rank lowest among focus areas on spending against sanction in 7/9 sampled districts [1-00596]. Bheden is the planning exception, with roads and sanitation leading [1-01807]. Ganjam and Rayagada are the spending exceptions: sanitation ranks lowest alongside maintenance of community systems in Ganjam and alongside GP office infrastructure in Rayagada [1-00596]. Water also stands out in Kalimela, where the Water Sufficient Village theme has the highest planned untied grant [1-01793].

Drinking water supply structures account for 47.8% [d1-46097] of the Water Sufficient Village theme’s recorded spending shortfall against sanction, or Rs 66.60 lakh below sanction [d1-46097][d1-03874]. Andhrua has the largest gap against sanction, at Rs 14.10 lakh [d1-03874], but the comparison covers only activities with a sanction on file—about one in six [d1-46097][d1-03874]. Against plans, spending on these structures is Rs 2.26 crore below plan [d1-03873], with the largest gaps in Laxmipur and Bandhpali [d1-03873]. Records with no sanctioning authority listed account for 69.8% [d1-04046] of that gap. Voucher-linked spending is spread across the sample, with Sharagada and Kalimela recording the largest amounts [d1-03870].

The records for abandoned works offer a focused reconciliation check: Chikilli and Govindapur account for all Rs 3.77 lakh [d1-03867] in planned amounts for abandoned drinking water supply works, and none of that amount has a sanctioning authority listed [d1-04040]. Separately, all spending labelled SC is recorded in Kalyansinghpur [d1-03872]; a possible swap between the SC and ST labels remains unconfirmed, so the two components should not be compared [d1-03872].

Against a recorded plan of Rs 5.35 crore [p-district-309-A3], Rs 2.33 crore was sanctioned [p-district-309-A4] and Rs 2.17 crore was spent [p-district-309-A5]. Spending was 40.5% of planned cost [p-district-309-A6], or Rs 3.18 crore below plan [p-district-309-A7].

The two Panchayats had similar shares of planned activities, but Govindapur had the larger share of planned cost, at 56.2% [d4-02523], while Dadhapatna had the larger share of spending, at 57.1% [d4-02525]. Roads alone accounted for 41.6% of planned untied grants [d1-14483]. In the separately reported general spending component, roads and drinking water had similar shares, at 24.2% and 22.7%, respectively [d1-14488].

Review the 2023-2024 records in particular: 275 activities from that year have no cost attached [p-district-309-B-2023-2024], and 95 works planned that year are marked abandoned [p-district-309-E3].

Spending was 25.2% of planned cost, below the middle value of 42.0% in the 20-Gram-Panchayat sample [p-gp-117835-A6]. Of its 640 planned activities [p-gp-117835-A1], 329 (51.4%) had no cost attached [p-gp-117835-A2][d1-29307].

Village infrastructure is a priority for the spending review: it accounted for 59.5% of planned cost [d1-29225] and 63.4% of the gap between plan and spending [d1-29231]. Check whether approvals exist outside the system. results.question: Findings on untied grant
results.tagged:
In the sample, Theme 6 – Self-sufficient Infrastructure in Village had the most untied grant funding planned in 18/20 Gram Panchayats [1-01793]. Boipariguda’s largest planned amount was under an unmapped theme, while Kalimela’s was under Theme 4 – Water Sufficient Village [1-01793]. Code 101 accounted for a majority of planned untied funding in 19/20 Gram Panchayats, with Boipariguda the only exception [1-01631]. Codes 101 and 105 were the leading output types in 18/20 Gram Panchayats [1-01817]; Boipariguda’s leading pair was Codes 101 and 103, and Haldikudar also differed [1-01817]. Maintenance and New/Fresh works led in 8/9 sampled districts, with Sundargarh the exception [1-00777].

The clearest records to reconcile are those with no sanctioning authority or scheme recorded. In 2023-2024, no sanctioning authority was recorded for Rs 16.48 crore [d1-18485], or 85.5% of planned untied funding for that year [d1-18485]. The same gap covered Rs 18.84 crore [d1-46978], or 62.6% of planned untied funding under Theme 6 [d1-46978], and Rs 6.73 crore [d1-28901], or 86.9% of Biswamathpur’s planned untied funding [d1-28901]. In Bheden, no scheme was recorded for Rs 4.37 crore [d1-28654], or 80.7% of its planned untied funding [d1-28654].

Boipariguda’s rural housing entries warrant a closer look: it accounted for Rs 2.13 crore [d1-24172], or 95.7% of the sample’s planned untied funding for rural housing [d1-24172], but only 2.0% of the activities in that focus area [d1-24172]. Planned funding recorded under the grant category “Other” was less concentrated: it totalled Rs 1.02 crore [d1-48094] across 8 Gram Panchayats [d1-48094], with Mendarajpur holding the largest share at 40.5% [d1-48094].

The Mixed social composition group accounted for a majority of planned untied funding in 5/6 fiscal years, with 2024-2025 the exception [1-00875]. Across all social composition groups, “ALL/ General public” and “General” were the leading categories for whom the work was intended [1-03030]. Separately, in recorded spending rather than plans, untied grants accounted for Rs 1.19 crore [d1-47425], or 88.3% of general-component spending under Theme 8 – Village with Good Governance [d1-47425].

results.question: What is happening with receipts?
results.tagged:
Across the 20 sampled Gram Panchayats, cashbooks recorded Rs 66.48 crore in receipts [d2-00001], and the sample contained 3,911 receipt vouchers [d2-00003]. No single Gram Panchayat dominated either measure: Andhrua had the largest share of money received at 10.2% [d2-00001], while Bheden had the largest share of receipt vouchers at 12.7% [d2-00003]. Within Bargarh’s sampled Gram Panchayats, however, Bheden accounted for 68.7% of receipt vouchers [d2-00648].

Receipt voucher counts fell from 816 in 2020-2021 [d2-01089] to 776 in 2021-2022 [d2-01103], 626 in 2022-2023 [d2-01180], 573 in 2023-2024 [d2-01320] and 555 in 2024-2025 [d2-01334], before edging up to 565 in 2025-2026 [d2-01474]. The amount received and the average amount per receipt both showed increases in monthly and quarterly comparisons, but neither showed a clear pattern at the fiscal-year level [2-00079][2-00078].

March is a useful starting point for checking receipt records. It accounted for 31.9% of the year’s vouchers in 2020-2021 [d2-01089], 61.3% in 2023-2024 [d2-01320] and 51.5% in 2025-2026 [d2-01474]. Mendarajpur also recorded its two highest monthly counts in March [d2-01867]. Both money received and voucher counts showed an annual seasonal pattern in 3/4 population bands, with Gram Panchayats of 10,000 people and above showing a different pattern [2-00276][2-00277]. The 2,500 to 5,000 and 5,000 to 10,000 bands led on both measures across all fiscal years [2-00267][2-00268].

At block level, Bhubaneswar led the sample in receipt voucher counts overall [d2-00010] and in money received in 4/6 fiscal years, with 2024-2025 and 2025-2026 the exceptions [2-00262]. Rangeilunda is worth a closer look in 2025-2026: it accounted for 28.7% of receipt vouchers, compared with 16.7% of all vouchers in the sample that year [d2-01418].

results.question: What has been found about training?
results.tagged:
In the 20-Gram-Panchayat sample, activities listed without a cost recorded 1,03,907 trainees [d1-36644], compared with 23,681 for costed activities [d1-36152]. Child Friendly Village accounted for 57.7% of trainees in costed activities [d1-36224]. Among activities listed without a cost, Child Friendly Village accounted for 35.5% [d1-36659], closely followed by Self-sufficient Infrastructure in Village at 33.5% [d1-36659]. Within the infrastructure theme, Health accounted for 51.5% of trainees (19,757 people) [d1-46839]. Across all social composition groups, Child Friendly Village led among themes [1-02911], Women and child development led among focus areas [1-02842], and activities listed as serving the general public accounted for most trainees [1-02491].

Some of the clearest concentrations were local. Bargarh accounted for 73.9% of trainees under Village with Good Governance (14,415 people) [d1-47287], while 2023-2024 accounted for 58.7% of the theme’s trainees (11,462 people) [d1-47545]. All 19,519 trainees under that theme were recorded under Poverty alleviation programme [d1-47309], split between Public Works (59.5%) and Beneficiary Oriented Programmes (40.5%) [d1-47373]. Under Water Sufficient Village, Dadhapatna alone accounted for 99.4% of trainees (1,200 people) [d1-45801].

Activities marked “Approved” accounted for most trainees in 17/20 Gram Panchayats; Barimunda, Boipariguda and Laxmipur showed no clear pattern [1-01678]. In the separate breakdown by sanctioning authority, all 152 trainees recorded against Gram Panchayat-sanctioned activities were under Technical training and vocational education [d1-41003].

Two gaps in the records limit what officials can trace: no fund component was recorded for any of the 50,577 trainees under Child Friendly Village [d1-45619], and no scheme was recorded for 19,512 of the 19,519 trainees under Village with Good Governance [d1-47482].

For voucher reconciliation, spending linked to a planned activity totalled Rs 3.26 crore in Khordha, with Andhrua accounting for the largest share [d2-00838], and Rs 2.07 crore in Cuttack, with Dadhapatna accounting for the largest share [d2-00719]. The share linked to planned activities rose from 2.7% to 53.2% across the six years covered [d2-00838][d2-00719]. That change should be read as more complete linking of records, not as evidence on its own that spending rose [d2-00838][d2-00719].
